title: 3D bioprinting of tissues and organs for systemic diseases and localized injuries
authors: W. Kee Ng; Paulo Bártolo
abstract: Three-dimensional (3D) bioprinting integrates engineering, materials science, and biology to fabricate living tissues with precise spatial control. By enabling the layer-by-layer deposition of cells and biomaterials, it overcomes many limitations of traditional scaffold-based tissue engineering and offers new opportunities for regenerative and personalized medicine. This review presents a comprehensive overview of recent advances in 3D bioprinting. It introduces a systematic, ASTM-aligned classification of key bioprinting modalities, extrusion, jetting, and vat photopolymerization, along with their respective material and biological design requirements. It also summarizes recent progress in bio-ink development and crosslinking strategies that improve print fidelity and functional tissue maturation. In addition, the review highlights applications in both systemic disease modelling and treatment (such as cardiovascular, endocrine/metabolic, and neurodegenerative disorders) and localized tissue repair (including skin, musculoskeletal, cartilage, and bone), emphasizing their relevance to civilian healthcare and military medicine. By combining technological innovation, biological insights, and regulatory considerations, this review outlines how advances in multi-modal bioprinting and intelligent process control can accelerate the translation of laboratory research into clinically viable, patient-specific therapies, driving the next generation of regenerative medicine.

title: Trial architecture in contemporary cardio-oncology: Why parallel-group randomized controlled trials may not fit every cardiotoxicity phenotype
authors: Radhia Chems Telli
abstract: Cardio-oncology has evolved rapidly with immune checkpoint inhibitors, chimeric antigen receptor T-cell therapies, antibody-drug conjugates, bispecific antibodies, and targeted kinase inhibitors, yet cardiovascular prevention strategies remain largely informed by evidence generated during the anthracycline era. This critical narrative review examines why cardioprotection trials have failed to keep pace with these evolving toxicity mechanisms, analyzing trial populations, endpoint selection, biomarker strategies, imaging approaches, and overall trial design across traditional and newer cancer therapies, rather than summarizing therapeutic efficacy. The evidence shows a persistent mismatch between contemporary toxicity phenotypes and existing trial design: Most studies continue to focus on anthracycline-associated left ventricular dysfunction and surrogate imaging endpoints, while immune-mediated myocarditis, cytokine release syndrome-related cardiomyopathy, vascular toxicities, arrhythmias, and other emerging phenotypes remain inadequately represented, compounded by limited biological stratification, one-size-fits-all prevention strategies, heterogeneous outcome definitions, and insufficient mechanism-specific monitoring. Progress in cardio-oncology prevention is constrained not only by the availability of candidate cardioprotective interventions but by the near-uniform persistence of a single trial architecture across mechanistically distinct toxicities. Future studies should adopt phenotype-driven, mechanism-informed, adaptive trial designs using clinically meaningful outcomes that reflect the diversity of contemporary cardiovascular toxicities.

title: Pacing in adults with complex congenital heart disease: A narrative minireview
authors: Vasileios Papaioannou; Julia Jones; Fahmi Faraz; David Mayhew; Archana Rao; Matthew Kahn; Sarah Moharem Elgamal; Reza Ashrafi
abstract: Congenital heart disease (CHD) is a growing health care problem, as more pediatric patients survive to adulthood every year as the number of patients with complex conditions also increases. As more patients survive, there has been an increase in the need for pacemaker procedures. Historically, there has been a focus on epicardial pacing in the most complex groups. In this review, we examine the background epidemiology, existing evidence for pacing, extraction data in three of the most complex CHD groups- transposition of the great arteries with an atrial switch procedure, patients palliated with a Fontan procedure and univentricular hearts. In this expert narrative review, we have used a broad search strategy of PubMed supplemented with evidence where available from non-congenital cohorts. The evidence in these most complex cohorts can be limited to expert centre opinion, small numbers and mixed paediatric/adult data. We discuss below the available data, the limitations and the novel approaches available in centres to deal with the most complex conditions such as conduction system pacing and leadless pacing with promising results albeit in expert centres only. Whilst current applicability to a wider range of institutions is not yet suggested by the paper, this review hopefully illustrates potential options for consideration and research in the future.

title: Cardiac comorbidity role in the diagnosis of diabetes mellitus using single lead electrocardiogram utilizing machine learning model
authors: Anna Dmitrievna Karbovskaya; Basheer Abdullah Marzoog; Snezhana Nikolaevna Demchuk; Anastasia Stroeva; Daniil Andreevich Zelenov; Peter Chomakhidze; Natalia Kuznetsova; Syrkin Abromavich; Valentin V Fadeev; Irina V. Poluboyarinova; Sevindzh M Ismailova; Philipp Kopylov
abstract: BACKGROUND Cardiovascular disease alters electrocardiographic morphology and may obscure diabetes-related electrical signatures, yet its effect on electrocardiogram (ECG)-based detection of type 1 and type 2 diabetes is poorly defined. AIM To investigate whether cardiac comorbidity differentially influences machine-learning detection of the two diabetes types from single-lead ECG. METHODS In this study, 2591 observations remained after exclusion of an erroneous age entry and rerunning the analytical pipeline. Twenty-six XGBoost models were evaluated separately for type 1 and type 2 diabetes within subgroups defined by seven cardiac-status criteria. Primary models used 47 single-lead ECG features and five anthropometric variables and were evaluated with five-fold stratified cross-validation. A post hoc seven-predictor sensitivity analysis assessed model complexity. Area under the receiver operating characteristics curve (AUC) uncertainty was estimated using 2000 bootstrap resamples of out-of-fold predictions, and ΔAUC comparisons were adjusted using the Benjamini-Hochberg procedure. Calibration was assessed using Brier score, calibration intercept and slope, reliability plots, and decision-curve analysis. Validation was observation-level because a persistent patient identifier was not available in the analytical export. RESULTS After correction and full rerun, median AUC was 0.693 for type 1 diabetes (range: 0.660-0.804) and 0.661 for type 2 diabetes (range: 0.543-0.716). No cardiac-pathology ΔAUC comparison remained statistically significant after Benjamini-Hochberg adjustment; the smallest adjusted P value was 0.064. In the reduced seven-predictor sensitivity analysis, AUC was higher than the 52-predictor model in 17 of 26 evaluable subgroup models, with a median descriptive difference of +0.008. Calibration was suboptimal: Across the 26 models, calibration slopes ranged from 0.078 to 0.467 and intercepts from -1.287 to -0.535. Decision-curve analysis showed threshold-dependent net benefit rather than uniform superiority across the evaluated range. CONCLUSION Single-lead ECG combined with anthropometric information showed moderate internal discrimination for recorded diabetes status, but the corrected analysis did not identify a cardiac-pathology subgroup effect that remained significant after multiplicity adjustment. The reduced-feature sensitivity analysis suggested that similar discrimination may be achievable with fewer predictors, whereas calibration remained inadequate for direct interpretation of model outputs as disease probabilities. These findings do not establish a clinically validated screening or rule-out threshold. Patient-grouped validation, independent threshold validation, and external validation remain necessary before clinical implementation.

title: Predicting Cardiopulmonary Exercise Testing Performance in Patients Undergoing Transthoracic Echocardiography - An AI-Based, Multimodal Model
authors: Shudhanshu Alishetti; Weishen Pan; Ashley Beecy; Zhenzhen Liu; Albert Gong; Zhe Huang; Kevin J. Clerkin; Ilan Richter; Rochelle L. Goldsmith; David T. Majure; Chris R. Kelsey; David vanMaanan; Jeffrey A. Ruhl; Naomi Tesfuzigta; Erica Lancet; Deepa Kumaraiah; Gabriel T. Sayer; Deborah L. Estrin; Kilian Weinberger; Volodymyr Kuleshov; Fei Wang; Nir Uriel
abstract: Abstract Background and Aims Cardiopulmonary exercise test (CPET) performance strongly correlates with survival in several disease states including heart failure, but has limited accessibility. Meanwhile, transthoracic echocardiography (TTE) is a far more widely available tool. We sought to develop an artificial intelligence (AI) algorithm using TTE and data from electronic medical records to predict CPET peak oxygen consumption (peak VO2) ≤ 14 mL/kg/min. Methods An AI model was trained to predict peak VO2 ≤14 mL/kg/min from TTE images, structured TTE reports, demographics, medications, labs, and vitals. The training set included patients with a TTE within 6 months of a CPET. Performance was retrospectively tested in a held-out group from the development cohort and an external regional validation cohort. Results 1,127 CPET studies paired with concomitant TTE were identified. The best performance was achieved by using all components (TTE images, all structured clinical data). The model performed well at predicting a peak VO2 ≤14 mL/kg/min, with an AUROC of 0.84 (development cohort) and 0.80 (external validation cohort). It performed consistently well using higher (≤18 mL/kg/min) and lower (≤12 mL/kg/min) cut-offs. Conclusions This multimodal AI model effectively categorized patients into low and high risk predicted peak VO2, demonstrating the potential to identify previously unrecognized high risk patients when CPET is not available.

title: Anemia and Iron Status in Pregnant and Postpartum Women With Acute Heart Failure
authors: Manisha Nair; Saswati Sanyal Choudhury; Augustin Sundar; Sereesha Rao; Gitanjali Deka; Carolin V. Solomi; Anjali Rani; Vijay Anand Ismavel; Swapna D. Kakoty; Pranabika Mahanta; Farzana Zahir; Indrani Roy; Rupanjali Deka; Charles Opondo; Megha Agarwal; Samuel Krasner; Paul Leeson; Samira Lakhal‐Littleton; Barbara Casadei; Jane Armitage
abstract: Importance In low- and middle-income countries (LMICs), iron-deficient anemia is highly prevalent and may compound the cardiovascular stress of pregnancy, yet its contribution to maternal acute heart failure (AHF) is poorly understood. Objectives To investigate the association of maternal anemia and iron status with AHF in pregnancy and post partum in India. Design, Setting, and Participants This multicenter, unmatched, prospective case-control study recruited participants from 10 hospitals across 4 Indian states from February 2019 to November 2024. Incident cases were pregnant or postpartum women with clinically diagnosed AHF. Controls were women without history or symptoms of heart disease within 48 hours post partum. Data were analyzed from March 2025 to April 2026. Exposures Maternal anemia and iron status. Blood samples collected at recruitment were analyzed for hemoglobin, ferritin, transferrin saturation, soluble transferrin receptor, and hepcidin. Main Outcomes and Measures The outcome of interest was AHF, defined using clinical criteria. Multivariable logistic regression models assessed associations of iron status and anemia with AHF, adjusting for potential confounders, including hypertensive disorders of pregnancy. Subgroup analyses were performed in women with echocardiographic abnormalities and peripartum cardiomyopathy. The discriminatory capacity of a model including anemia present before AFH onset vs a model with established risk factors only was examined using receiver operating characteristic curves. Results Among 532 women with clinically diagnosed AHF (median [IQR] age, 25 [21-29] years) and 1091 controls (median [IQR] age, 25 [21-28] years), moderate and severe anemia were associated with 1.5-fold (adjusted odds ratio [aOR], 1.52; 95% CI, 1.13-2.05) and 5-fold (aOR, 5.06; 95% CI, 3.02-8.48) increased odds of AHF, respectively, compared with women without anemia. Higher soluble transferrin receptor levels (aOR, 1.44; 95% CI, 1.31-1.57) and the lowest hepcidin quintile (aOR, 2.65; 95% CI, 1.69-4.14), both indicative of iron deficiency, were independently associated with AHF. These associations persisted after adjusting for hypertensive disorders of pregnancy and after excluding women with preexisting cardiac conditions, and they were consistent in subgroups with echocardiographic abnormalities and peripartum cardiomyopathy. Adding anemia to established risk factors improved model discrimination for identifying AHF risk, increasing the AUC from 78% (95% CI, 76%-81%) to 83% (95% CI, 80%-85%) ( P < .001). Conclusion and Relevance This case-control study found that maternal anemia and iron deficiency were independently associated with AHF during pregnancy and post partum. Further studies are needed to determine whether preventing or treating iron deficiency and anemia can reduce AHF risk and improve maternal outcomes.

title: Right ventricular function among adult survivors of childhood cancer
authors: Tomáš Sláma; Reto Kurmann; Eva Haegler‐Laube; Gabriela M. Kuster; Nana Kwabena Poku; Eva Scheler; Claudia Elisabeth Kuehni; Nicolas von der Weid; Christina Schindera
abstract: Abstract Background : Cardiotoxic effects of childhood cancer treatment on the right ventricle (RV) are sparsely studied among long-term childhood cancer survivors (CCS). Objectives : We investigated RV function and risk factors for impaired function. Methods : We invited CCS ≥18 years of age, diagnosed between ages 0–20 years, treated in one of five pediatric oncology centers across Switzerland from 1976–2017, who survived ≥5 years, for an echocardiographic assessment of the RV including tricuspid annular plane systolic excursion (TAPSE, abnormal <17mm) and Doppler tissue imaging (DTI, abnormal <9.5cm/s). Results : We included 432 CCS with median age at study of 34 years (interquartile range 26–40). Overall prevalence of RV dysfunction was 4% for both methods (mean TAPSE 22.5±3.8mm; mean DTI 13.1±2.2cm/s). Risk factors for decreased RV function were cumulative heart-relevant radiotherapy (RT) dose [Beta coefficient (B)=-0.46;95%CI -0.73– -0.20]; hematopoietic stem cell transplantation (B=-1.88;95%CI -3.35– -0.40); cisplatin (B=-1.29;95%CI -2.38– -0.19); diabetes mellitus (B=-2.57;95%CI -4.99– -0.15); and abdominal obesity (B=-0.79;95%CI -1.58–0.00) when measured by TAPSE. For DTI, we identified cumulative heart-relevant RT dose (B=-0.19; 95%CI -0.37– -0.01); relapse (B=-0.94;95%CI -1.74– -0.15); and abdominal obesity (B=-0.80;95%CI -1.37– -0.24) as risk factors. Cumulative anthracycline dose was not associated with impaired RV function measured by TAPSE (B=-0.23;95%CI -0.49–0.03) or DTI (B=-0.06;95%CI -0.25–0.13). Conclusions : RV dysfunction is rare in young adult CCS. The risk is increased after heart-relevant RT and by obesity. Given the prognostic value of RV dysfunction for all-cause mortality, we suggest including RV echocardiography to the routine follow-up care of CCS.

title: Management of a pregnant woman with symptomatic severe rheumatic mitral stenosis and severe pulmonary hypertension: a case report
authors: Hasan Haghaninejad; Mojtaba Jokar; Abolfazl Yavari
abstract: Rheumatic heart disease (RHD), and especially mitral stenosis (MS), remains an important cause of maternal cardiovascular morbidity and mortality in low and middle-income countries. A 34-year-old woman with a history of rheumatic MS presented at 14 weeks of gestational age with progressive dyspnea (NYHA functional class III). Echocardiography showed severe MS with severe pulmonary hypertension. Termination was discussed due to high maternal risk with continuation of pregnancy but the patient declined after counseling regarding maternal and fetal risks. Later at 18 weeks of gestation percutaneous transvenous mitral commissurotomy (PTMC) was suggested but was also declined. Therefore, the patient was managed with individualized medical therapy with dose adjustment and close clinical and echocardiographic follow-up. Her symptoms improved from NYHA functional class III to class II and she remained clinically stable until elective cesarean delivery at 36 weeks and 4 days in a tertiary-care center. There was not any maternal complication in pregnancy, delivery or early post-partum period and not immediate complication in the newborn. This case highlights the need for individualized medical management and careful follow-up in cases where recommended interventions are declined and that a favorable outcome in one case does not replace guideline recommended treatment.

title: Speckle-tracking echocardiographic strain parameters in cardiac magnetic resonance–confirmed myocarditis: associations with myocardial edema and subsequent left ventricular functional improvement
authors: Shelley Lauren Cham; Joseph Raymond Cuaresma; Renato C. Ong; Jamelen R. Narvasa
abstract: Abstract Background Cardiac magnetic resonance (CMR) is the noninvasive reference standard for diagnosing myocarditis and assessing myocardial inflammation, but its routine use may be limited by availability, cost, and patient-related factors. Speckle-tracking echocardiography may provide an accessible approach to evaluating myocardial dysfunction and outcomes. This study aimed to evaluate the associations of global longitudinal strain (GLS), peak atrial longitudinal strain (PALS), and time-to-peak longitudinal strain (TPLS) with CMR-defined myocardial edema, biomarkers, and subsequent left ventricular (LV) functional improvement in patients with CMR-confirmed myocarditis. Methods This single-center ambispective observational cohort study included 40 adults with CMR-confirmed myocarditis and baseline echocardiography suitable for strain analysis. Cross-sectional associations between baseline strain parameters, CMR findings, and biomarkers were assessed, with longitudinal evaluation of subsequent LV functional improvement among patients with follow-up echocardiography. Receiver operating characteristic and regression analyses were exploratory; data-derived thresholds were not internally or externally validated. Results Among 40 patients with CMR-confirmed myocarditis, TPLS ≥ 447 ms showed 52.4% sensitivity and 86.7% specificity for CMR-defined myocardial edema (area under the curve [AUC], 0.58). The combined GLS-TPLS model showed 81.0% sensitivity, 53.3% specificity, 69.4% accuracy, and an AUC of 0.64. GLS and PALS correlated inversely with peak N-terminal pro–B-type natriuretic peptide (NT-proBNP; r = –0.438, P = 0.006 and r = –0.396, P = 0.017, respectively). Thirty-five patients had evaluable longitudinal LV ejection fraction (LVEF) measurements; 11 (31.4%) met criteria for LV functional improvement. Baseline GLS was associated with subsequent LV functional improvement, although interpretation is limited by its strong relationship with baseline LVEF. Conclusions In CMR-confirmed myocarditis, strain parameters provided complementary functional information across imaging, biomarker, and longitudinal domains. TPLS was associated with CMR-defined myocardial edema, while GLS and PALS were associated with NT-proBNP. Baseline GLS was associated with subsequent LV functional improvement. These exploratory findings support prospective evaluation of strain alongside CMR and development of multimodal risk stratification models in larger, controlled cohorts.

title: Cardiac amyloidosis masked by anchoring bias in a patient with repaired atrial septal defect: a case report
authors: Yan Jiang; Tian Zhang; 马小静
abstract: Abstract Background: Cardiac amyloidosis (CA) is an infiltrative cardiomyopathy that frequently mimics other cardiac conditions and is easily overlooked once a structural cardiac diagnosis has been established. We report a case of systemic lambda light-chain (AL) amyloidosis unmasked four years after surgical repair of an atrial septal defect (ASD), highlighting the diagnostic anchoring bias that delayed recognition. Case presentation: A 75-year-old woman presented with refractory heart failure four years after surgical repair of an ASD. Her progressively worsening symptoms had been attributed solely to the pre-existing structural heart disease. On readmission, transthoracic echocardiography demonstrated biatrial enlargement, severe mitral and tricuspid regurgitation, biventricular wall thickening with a granular sparkling appearance, and a small pericardial effusion. Three-dimensional speckle-tracking echocardiography revealed profoundly reduced left ventricular global longitudinal strain (GLS, -6.0%) with relative apical sparing, and reduced right ventricular free-wall longitudinal strain (-8.1%). Electrocardiography showed atrial fibrillation, intraventricular conduction delay, and poor precordial R-wave progression. Serum immunofixation electrophoresis detected a lambda-type monoclonal protein, with a markedly elevated free lambda light chain and a decreased kappa/lambda ratio. Abdominal fat pad biopsy showed Congo red-positive amyloid deposits, and electron microscopy revealed rigid, non-branching amyloid fibrils measuring 8-12 nm in diameter, confirming systemic AL amyloidosis. According to the revised Mayo 2012 staging system (NT-proBNP 29,218 pg/mL), she was classified as stage III. The patient declined bone marrow biopsy and clone-directed chemotherapy and was transferred to another hospital for further management. Conclusions: Once a structural cardiac diagnosis is established, clinicians are prone to anchoring bias and may overlook coexisting infiltrative disease. In patients with refractory or progressive heart failure after correction of structural heart disease, systematic reassessment-including strain echocardiography, monoclonal protein screening, and tissue biopsy-should be pursued to unmask CA and enable timely, potentially life-prolonging therapy.

title: Peripartum Cardiomyopathy
authors: K Sliwa; D Hilfiker-Kleiner; A Damasceno; H Al Farhan; Sonel Goland; MR Johnson; J Bauersachs
abstract: ( Lancet . 2025;406(10518):2483–2493. doi:10.1016/S0140-6736(25)01451-5) Peripartum cardiomyopathy (PPCM) is a serious and potentially fatal form of heart failure that develops toward the end of pregnancy or in the months following delivery in women with no prior history of heart disease. Over the past 2 decades, increased recognition and research have substantially advanced understanding of its causes, diagnosis, and management. The condition is defined by the presence of left ventricular systolic dysfunction, typically an ejection fraction below 45%, after exclusion of alternative explanations such as congenital, valvular, or pre-existing cardiomyopathies. Despite therapeutic progress, PPCM remains associated with significant maternal and neonatal morbidity and mortality, and only about half of affected women experience full recovery of cardiac function within 6 months.

title: Case Report: Giant left main coronary artery aneurysm complicated by recurrent coronary thrombosis in a patient with metastatic pancreatic adenocarcinoma
authors: Maciej Południewski; Monika Amielan; Izabela Kruszewska; Ryszard Jabłoński; Artur Dubicki; Sławomir Dobrzycki
abstract: Coronary artery aneurysms and ectasia are uncommon coronary abnormalities associated with disturbed coronary flow and an increased risk of thrombosis. Their management becomes particularly challenging in patients with active malignancy, in whom both thrombotic and bleeding risks are substantially increased. We report a 55-year-old male patient with metastatic pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma admitted with NSTEMI. Coronary angiography revealed a giant LMCA aneurysm, significant LMCA/LAD disease, and chronic total occlusion of the RCA. Given the advanced malignancy and initial clinical stabilization, a multidisciplinary Heart Team selected a conservative strategy. Two months later, the patient was readmitted with chest pain and dyspnea and was diagnosed with segmental pulmonary embolism. Three hours later, an anterior STEMI developed due to thrombosis of the LMCA aneurysm and thrombotic LAD occlusion, requiring urgent LMCA/LAD PCI with two drug-eluting stents. On day 5, subacute LAD stent thrombosis required repeat PCI with balloon angioplasty. This case illustrates the challenges of balancing ischemic, thrombotic, and bleeding risks in patients with coronary artery aneurysms and active malignancy and highlights the importance of individualized multidisciplinary decision-making.

title: Association between elevated body mass index and new-onset heart failure in patients undergoing catheter ablation for atrial fibrillation
authors: Adham Ramadan; Mohamed Doma; Ghazal Sanadgol; Mohammad Hosein Yazdanpanah; Acile Nahlawi; Marawan Desouky; Leon M. Ptaszek; Jeremy N. Ruskin
abstract: Background Atrial fibrillation (AF) is the most common arrhythmia and a major contributor to heart failure (HF). While catheter ablation (CA) reduces HF progression, some patients remain at risk for incident HF after ablation. This study aims to analyze the relationship between body mass index (BMI) and new-onset HF in patients undergoing CA for AF. Methods We retrospectively studied patients from the MGH Research Patient Data Registry who underwent first-time CA for AF from January 2013 to August 2024. The primary outcome was new-onset HF. Cox regression identified independent predictors, and Kaplan–Meier analysis assessed HF-free survival across BMI categories. Results Among 7,363 patients, 550 (7.5%) developed HF during 3.6 ± 2.9 years of follow-up. HF-free survival declined across increasing BMI categories. At 10 years, HF-free survival was 94.2% for BMI <25 and 86.3% for BMI ≥40. Independent predictors of HF included age ≥75 years (HR 1.79, 95% CI 1.45–2.22), female sex (HR 1.41, 95% CI 1.16–1.73), hypertension (HR 1.28, 95% CI 1.03–1.59), ischemic heart disease (HR 1.44, 95% CI 1.19–1.74), mitral regurgitation (HR 2.60, 95% CI 2.07–3.27), aortic stenosis (HR 1.97, 95% CI 1.38–2.80), pulmonary hypertension (HR 3.02, 95% CI 2.26–4.05), pulmonary embolism (HR 1.99, 95% CI 1.23–3.21), eGFR <60 (HR 2.51, 95% CI 1.87–3.37), BMI 30–34.99 (HR 1.41, 95% CI 1.08–1.85), BMI 35–39.99 (HR 1.90, 95% CI 1.38–2.62), and BMI ≥40 (HR 2.31, 95% CI 1.56–3.41). Conclusions Elevated BMI is independently associated with new-onset HF after AF ablation, with risk rising progressively across BMI categories. These patients may warrant continued attention to cardiovascular risk after ablation.

title: Advancing a FAIR and explainable AI-based predictive model for cardiovascular diseases in hospital settings
authors: Adina Niţulescu
abstract: The healthcare field is witnessing an increasing volume of data available for analysis and is undergoing pragmatic transformations due to the advent of artificial intelligence. In recent years, machine learning and its sub-field, deep learning have emerged as effective tools to help physicians with diagnosis, predictions and improved treatment plans. The paper describes a cohort of patients which were monitored during their regular visits in the cardiology department of the County Emergency Clinical Hospital of Timis in Romania on their physiological parameters and test results. After employing a wide range of conventional machine learning and advanced deep learning techniques, the experimental results revealed that the feedforward neural network performed best in predicting cardiovascular outcomes. The paper also analyzes the aspects of FAIR AI, which translates to the usage of artificial intelligence in a ethical and unbiased way in order to improve the early and precise diagnosis for cardiac patients. The work presented in this paper represents an overview of the current situation in CVDs management and treatment options, as well as offering a viable and interoperable AI-based solution that can be integrated in cardiology hospital departments in order to improve the diagnosis and experience of cardiac patients.

title: A combined systemic inflammation score for predicting long-term mortality in patients admitted to the intensive cardiovascular care unit
authors: Abed Qadan; Ziv Dadon; Louay Taha; Dov Gavish; Mohammad Karmi; Pierre François Sabouret; Nour Karra; Ari Naimark; Mamas A. Mamas; Noam Fink; Rana Al Hamori; Akiva Brin; Dana Deeb; Rafel Hitter; Hila Gerard; Netanel Zacks; Amjad Abu-Salman; Michael Glikson; Elad Asher
abstract: Background Systemic inflammation contributes to the development of cardiovascular disease, but whether admission inflammatory biomarker levels predict long-term prognosis in critically ill cardiac patients remains debated. Methods We conducted a large, single-center observational study of consecutive ICCU admissions (January 2020–December 2021). Six biomarkers were evaluated for their ability to predict long-term all-cause mortality (median follow-up 4.7 years in the derivation cohort and 3.2 years in the validation cohort): neutrophil-to-lymphocyte ratio (NLR), platelet-to-lymphocyte ratio (PLR), systemic immune-inflammation index (SII), C-reactive protein-to-albumin ratio (CAR), fibrinogen-to-albumin ratio index (FARI), and immature platelet fraction (IPF). Optimal cutoffs were derived with receiver operating characteristic (ROC) analysis and the Youden index, and were then tested in an independent temporal validation cohort from the same center (2022 ICCU admissions). A composite score was built from the markers that remained significant in multivariable analysis. Results The derivation cohort included 2,131 patients and the validation cohort 1,013. Higher admission levels of most biomarkers were associated with higher long-term mortality. After multivariable adjustment, NLR (HR 1.68), SII (HR 1.40), CAR (HR 1.94), and FARI (HR 1.72) remained independent predictors of long-term mortality, beyond traditional risk factors. The composite score showed stepwise risk separation in unadjusted analysis; after adjustment, only scores of 3 and 4 remained independently associated with mortality (HR 2.58 and 3.31, respectively). Conclusions Elevated admission levels of NLR, SII, CAR, and FARI independently predicted long-term mortality in ICCU patients and may help refine risk assessment before discharge. A composite score based on these markers identified patients at the highest risk, but it did not reliably separate intermediate-risk groups. Further prospective studies, including external validation, are warranted.

title: Impact of cardiac phase selection on the diagnostic performance of CT-FFR: the role of myocardial bridging and heart rate
authors: Jianhui Song; Jie Zhou; QIYU ZHANG; FANG ZHANG; WEI GAO; YAN XIA; J Y Ma; Rende Xu; LEILEI MA; JUYING QIAN; CHENGUANG LI; JUNBO GE
abstract: Computed tomography-derived fractional flow reserve (CT-FFR) is commonly calculated from diastolic-phase coronary CT angiography, but phase selection may be affected by high heart rate and myocardial bridging. We compared CT-FFR derived from systolic- and diastolic-phase reconstructions and explored phase-related differences according to myocardial bridging and heart rate. This retrospective, single-center diagnostic-accuracy study included 138 patients contributing 155 vessels examined using a second-generation single-source 320-detector-row CT platform. CT-FFR was calculated separately from diastolic- and systolic-phase reconstructions using the same steady-state computational framework. Invasive FFR and CT-FFR values ≤ 0.80 were considered positive. Analyses of the invasive-FFR-defined grey zone (0.75–0.85), myocardial bridging, heart-rate groups (≤ 70 vs. > 70 beats/min), and subgroup interactions were post hoc and exploratory. Diastolic-reconstruction-derived CT-FFR showed higher overall discrimination than systolic-reconstruction-derived CT-FFR (AUC, 0.91 vs. 0.87; difference, 0.039; patient-clustered bootstrap 95% CI, 0.006–0.072). Diagnostic correctness did not differ significantly after accounting for within-patient clustering (OR, 1.18; 95% CI, 0.84–1.67; P = 0.346). In the invasive-FFR-defined grey zone, paired accuracy was 78.4% versus 56.9% (difference, 21.6% points; 95% CI, 4.5–37.0; exact McNemar P = 0.027). In vessels with myocardial bridging, the observed AUC was higher for diastolic than systolic reconstruction (0.90 vs. 0.79; P = 0.011), with an exploratory phase-by-myocardial-bridging interaction (OR, 2.72; 95% CI, 1.07–6.92; P = 0.036). In the heart-rate > 70 beats/min subgroup, no significant phase difference or phase-by-heart-rate interaction was detected. Diastolic-phase reconstruction showed slightly higher overall discrimination, whereas threshold-based diagnostic correctness was similar after accounting for clustering. Myocardial bridging may modify phase-related performance, but heart-rate-stratified findings remain hypothesis-generating.

title: Systemic Inflammatory Indices and CRP-to-Albumin Ratio in Association with Restenosis Following Percutaneous Mitral Balloon Valvuloplasty: An Observational Cohort Study-Uncorrected Proof
authors: Cemre Turgul; Fuat Polat; Aigul Zhusupova; Ali Doğan; Ramazan Topsakal; Cuma Süleymanoğlu
journal: Turk Kardiyoloji Dernegi Arsivi-Archives of the Turkish Society of Cardiology
abstract: OBJECTIVE: Percutaneous mitral balloon valvuloplasty (PMBV) is the treatment of choice for suitable patients with rheumatic mitral stenosis, but restenosis remains clinically relevant. This study evaluated whether preprocedural inflammatory indices are associated with restenosis after PMBV. METHOD: We retrospectively evaluated 141 consecutive patients who underwent successful PMBV. Preprocedural neutrophil-to-lymphocyte ratio (NLR), platelet-to-lymphocyte ratio (PLR), monocyte-to-lymphocyte ratio (MLR), systemic immune-inflammation index (SII), systemic inflammatory response index (SIRI), C-reactive protein (CRP), CRP-to-albumin ratio (CAR), and serum uric acid were assessed. Restenosis was defined as a mitral valve area (MVA) <1.5 cm² during follow-up. Kaplan-Meier and Cox regression analyses were used as the primary analyses. Logistic regression with 1,000-bootstrap internal validation was performed as a secondary analysis. Multivariable models were adjusted for the Wilkins score and relevant clinical covariates. RESULTS: During a median follow-up of 36 months (IQR, 28-44), restenosis occurred in 33 patients (23.4%). PLR, MLR, CAR, and uric acid levels were higher in patients with restenosis after false discovery rate correction (all q<0.05). In the multivariable Cox analysis, the Wilkins score was the sole independent predictor of restenosis (HR, 2.14; 95% CI, 1.43-3.20; P < 0.001), whereas CAR (HR, 1.18; 95% CI, 0.94-1.49; P = 0.16) and uric acid (HR, 1.09; 95% CI, 0.91-1.30; P = 0.34) were not independently associated with restenosis. CAR demonstrated an AUC of 0.71 (95% CI, 0.61-0.81). Adding CAR to the Wilkins score did not improve discrimination (ΔAUC=0.02; NRI=0.11, P = 0.26; IDI=0.019, P = 0.11). CONCLUSION: The Wilkins score was the sole independent predictor of restenosis after PMBV. Preprocedural CAR and uric acid were associated with restenosis in unadjusted analyses but provided no independent or incremental prognostic value beyond established clinical and echocardiographic factors.

title: Clinical outcomes of apixaban in patients with atrial fibrillation and very high thromboembolic risk (CHA₂DS₂-VASc ≥5): a retrospective cohort study
authors: Abrar F. Alshehri; Abdullah S. Alshammari; Shaimaa Alsulami; Tamim N. Alkhaldi; Qussi H. Basranah; Saud A. Hijazi; Fatimah M. Hamdi; Saleh Alghamdi; Asma M. Alshahrani; Emad Elkholy; Mohammed A. Alnuhait; Mohammed Abdulrahman Alrashed
abstract: Abstract Background Real-world evidence on apixaban in patients with atrial fibrillation (AF) at very high thromboembolic risk (CHA₂DS₂-VASc ≥ 5) is limited, particularly from the Middle East. We compared clinical outcomes between apixaban-treated patients with CHA₂DS₂-VASc scores ≥ 5 and 0–4, and between prescribed doses within the very high-risk group. Methods In this retrospective cohort study at a tertiary referral center in Makkah, Saudi Arabia, adults with AF treated with apixaban between January 2019 and December 2024 were grouped by baseline CHA₂DS₂-VASc score. Outcomes were documented thromboembolic events, bleeding of any severity, and in-hospital mortality. Odds ratios (ORs) were estimated by unadjusted and multivariable logistic regression. A sensitivity analysis excluded patients with a recorded prior stroke. Results Of 596 patients, 175 (29.4%) had scores ≥ 5. Thromboembolic events (31.4% vs 7.1%; adjusted OR 6.6, 95% CI 3.9–11.0) and in-hospital mortality (14.3% vs 1.7%; adjusted OR 7.7, 95% CI 3.2–18.5) were more frequent with scores ≥ 5, whereas bleeding did not differ significantly (54.9% vs 46.8%; adjusted OR 1.3, 95% CI 0.9–1.9). Of 68 patients with a recorded prior stroke, 58 also had a documented thromboembolic event; after their exclusion, thromboembolic events no longer differed (5.2% vs 5.1%), whereas bleeding (adjusted OR 3.2, 95% CI 2.0–5.1) and mortality (adjusted OR 8.7, 95% CI 3.4–22.1) were more frequent with scores ≥ 5. Among very high-risk patients, prescribed dose (2.5 mg, n = 73; 5 mg, n = 102, twice daily) was not significantly associated with any outcome. Conclusions A CHA₂DS₂-VASc score ≥ 5 was associated with higher in-hospital mortality among apixaban-treated patients with AF. The excess of thromboembolic events was confined to patients with a recorded prior stroke and may reflect overlap between baseline history and outcome recording. Prescribed dose was not associated with outcomes, although dose appropriateness could not be assessed. Larger studies with complete dosing criteria and event timing are needed.

title: Risk factors for postoperative low cardiac output syndrome (LCOS) in patients with giant left ventricular valvular heart disease and its correlation with preoperative LVEF
authors: Wang Beibei; Zhenkun Yu; Ting Wang
abstract: To investigate the risk factors for postoperative low cardiac output syndrome (LCOS) in patients with giant left ventricle and valvular heart disease. Left ventricular ejection fraction (LVEF) was identified as a key predictor of LCOS. Accordingly, Pearson correlation analysis was performed to examine the association between preoperative LVEF and postoperative mean arterial pressure in this patient population. A retrospective cohort of 135 patients with giant left ventricular valvular heart disease admitted to our institution between December 2023 and January 2025 was enrolled in this study. All patients underwent heart valve replacement surgery and were subsequently categorized into the LCOS group and non-LCOS group according to the occurrence of postoperative LCOS. Baseline characteristics and disease-related variables were collected for both groups. Variables with significant differences were analyzed using a logistic regression model to identify independent risk factors for postoperative LCOS. Receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curves and Pearson correlation analysis were subsequently applied to evaluate the predictive value of the identified risk factors for postoperative LCOS. Pearson correlation analysis revealed that preoperative LVEF was correlated with postoperative mean arterial pressure in patients with giant left ventricle and valvular heart disease. Among the 135 enrolled patients, 30 developed postoperative LCOS. The mean arterial pressure was (56.15 ± 3.76) mmHg in the LCOS group and (62.24 ± 3.81) mmHg in the non-LCOS group. Significant differences were observed between the two groups in cardiopulmonary bypass (CPB) time, intraoperative blood loss, preoperative renal insufficiency, mean pulmonary artery pressure (mPAP), and LVEF (all P < 0.05). LASSO-logistic regression analysis identified CPB time, preoperative renal insufficiency, mPAP, and LVEF as independent risk factors for postoperative LCOS in patients with giant left ventricular valvular heart disease ( P < 0.05, OR > 1). ROC curve, calibration curve, and decision curve analyses demonstrated that the combined model incorporating these variables exhibited favorable predictive performance for postoperative LCOS. Pearson correlation analysis demonstrated that preoperative LVEF was correlated with postoperative mean arterial pressure in patients with giant left ventricular valvular heart disease. Multiple factors influence the development of postoperative LCOS in patients with giant left ventricular valvular heart disease, including CPB time, preoperative renal insufficiency, mPAP, and LVEF. Targeted clinical interventions should be implemented to mitigate risk and improve postoperative recovery.

title: Comparison of Adverse Event Incidence between Japanese and Non-Japanese: A Systematic Review and Meta-analysis for Patients with Rheumatoid Arthritis, Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease, and Atrial Fibrillation/Venous Thromboembolism
authors: Satomi SAKURAI; Kazuhiro Matsui; Mamoru Narukawa
abstract: Enhancing diversity in clinical trial populations is increasingly important, particularly for underrepresented populations. We focused on adverse events (AEs) that have been reported to be more frequent in Japanese than in non-Japanese populations and assessed their plausibility. We conducted a systematic review and random-effects meta-analysis of 24 multiregional clinical trials (MRCTs): 9 in rheumatoid arthritis (RA), 11 in chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), and 4 in atrial fibrillation (AF) or venous thromboembolism (VTE). Pooled estimates of the odds ratios (ORs) compared the incidence of targeted AEs between Japanese and non-Japanese participants using a random-effects model. For Janus kinase inhibitors in RA, the OR for the incidence of herpes zoster was 2.50 (95% confidence interval [CI]: 1.18–5.29, p = 0.0172), suggesting more frequent occurrence in Japanese participants than in non-Japanese participants. The incidence of pneumonia was statistically higher in Japanese in most COPD treatment groups and in the placebo group (OR 4.03 [95% CI: 1.33–12.19, p = 0.0135] for placebo). For direct oral anticoagulants for AF/VTE, the OR for major bleeding was 1.19 (95% CI: 0.91–1.56, p = 0.2105), with no statistically significant difference observed between Japanese and non-Japanese participants. This meta-analysis supported a higher incidence of herpes zoster in Japanese patients with RA, whereas the findings for pneumonia in COPD should be interpreted cautiously, and no statistically significant difference was observed for major bleeding in AF/VTE. Broader inclusion of Japanese participants in MRCTs may improve the interpretability of safety findings and the understanding of population-related differences in drug safety profiles.
